full_narrative: Traditional Wampanoag oral history describes Maushop as a benevolent giant who inhabited the coastal timber and created islands. Known for his immense size, deep voice audible across water, and preference for solitary wilderness areas.
Wampanoag elders speak of small, hair-covered beings inhabiting dense cedar swamps. Noted for throwing rocks at trespassers, wood knocking, and mimicking animal whistles at dusk to confuse travelers.

Origin of the anglicized name 'Sasquatch' in the Halq'eméylem language. Described as elusive, hair-covered mountain dwellers who serve as guardians of the forest, communicating via tree knocks and whistling.
Koyukon oral histories describe solitary wild men living along dense taiga river valleys. Known to forage at night near salmon runs and leave oversized footprints in mud banks.
Klamath tradition speaks of tall bipedal forest dwellers in the mountain passes. Noted for tree shaking, throwing rocks down ravines, and keeping watch over high elevation wilderness boundaries.
Recorded in ancient tribal pictographs in the Sierra foothills. Described as large, hair-covered bipedal protectors of oak groves and river canyons who avoid human contact.
Choctaw traditional lore speaks of the Shampe, an ill-smelling, hair-covered giant of the dense river swamps who avoids daylight and possesses great physical strength.
Makah coastal accounts describe night-roaming forest dwellers who travel in the fog, wood knock near timber lines, and slip past villages without leaving a trace.
Lakota elders speak of Chiye-Tanka ('Big Elder Brother'), a hairy giant inhabiting river coulees. Viewed as a spiritual warning figure teaching respect for untamed nature.
